newsitem.title: USA: US CREDIT OUTLOOK--Jobless, waiting for payrolls.
newsitem.headline: US CREDIT OUTLOOK--Jobless, waiting for payrolls.

text.p: The U.S. Treasury market gets two economic reports on Thursday but the main influence on the penultimate trading session of the week -- the monthly U.S. employment report -- will not be released until Friday.

"People are just waiting for Friday morning," said Josh Feinman, vice president and global markets economist at Bankers Trust. "Having said that, the claims numbers are very important. The trend there has been pretty unmistakable; there's a very low level of jobless claims, indicating a very strong labor market," he said. "We'll see if that continues."

Jobless claims numbers for the week ended March 1, due at 0830 EST/1330 GMT, are estimated to have totaled 317,000, according to a Reuters poll of economists, little changed from the level of 316,000 new jobless claims a week earlier.

Because monetary policymakers frequently remark on the strength of the labor market, bond traders and economists will pay much more attention to the jobless claims figures than to January factory orders data, due at 1000 EST/1500 GMT.
January factory orders are forecast to be up 2.0 percent after December's 1.3 percent drop.

"The most important stuff is the claims data," said Matthew Alexy, chief market strategist at Credit Suisse First Boston. "The factory orders are a recap and re-mix of other data, much of which the market has already seen."

Dana Johnson, managing director and head of research at First Chicago Capital Markets Inc., said that Thursday's trading session mainly will be a matter of "waiting for (February) payrolls" data on Friday.
But he said all the evidence of labor market tightness means there will be "understandable interest" in the jobless claims data on Thursday.

"What's important about the claims information is what's going on with the number of people who remain unemployed," said James Glassman, senior economist at Chase Securities Inc. "The number of people who don't get recalled to work is trending down and has been on a downward trajectory since this time a year ago," said Glassman. "With new jobless claims at low levels, that means that fewer people are getting laid off than are getting recalled. That just confirms that the job market is in pretty good shape," he said.
Even if the jobless claims data on Thursday reinforce the picture of a strong labor market, bond prices could rise, said Johnson.
Johnson said players could spend Thursday squaring positions before the monthly jobless report on Friday.
"There's a sense that there are more short positions out there than long positions so position squaring might give the market a lift," he said.
The benchmark 30-year Treasury bond ended at 97-14/32 on Wednesday, up 17/32 to yield 6.83 percent.
Dealers indicated that Federal funds would open at 5-3/16 percent on Thursday.
